advances: There is a quantitative global charge for every positive midpoint-logconcave law and every selection of rows in the three-point parity setting. Its coefficient is controlled by outward expansion of the actual midpoint graph, and hence by the squared Euclidean radius of the finite support. This proves that finite geometry eliminates exact resonance and identifies the quantitative information lost when one only uses the local scalar energy. The coefficient need not be dimension-free. For uniform laws the dimension-free intensity charge is equivalent to a positive absolute gap between the support size and three times the number of ambient parity classes. The accepted vertex budget does not provide that gap, and the accepted near-saturation criterion would violate it if its unproved apex existence hypothesis were fulfilled. One sharply stated further test is whether there is an absolute \(c>0\) such that every nonempty set \(B\) of nontrivial centers in every support satisfying the hypotheses below has at least \(c|B|\) directed endpoint incidences leaving \(B\). A positive answer supplies the full weighted charge through this lemma; no apex search or local algebraic configuration is offered as a counterexample.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Accepted fact ee640ebdfbcb632d is used for the unchanged canonical normalization and target charge. Accepted facts 768d9712b73c4ab7 and 3dd581471de351a8 provide the stated finite calibrations. Accepted facts 44636aeaf6af4b6c and 4e40b39340899863 provide the vertex-defect comparison and the explicitly conditional lift criterion. All new graph expansion, weighted charge, uniform equivalence, and coefficient-degeneration assertions are proved above.
proof:
First establish the graph and reflection accounting. A distinct reflected pair with integer center has equal-parity endpoints, so conditions (ii)-(iii) imply that every nontrivial row has exactly the three atoms \(\lbrace u_j,j,v_j\rbrace\) for one \(j\in\mathcal J\), and every other supported row is a singleton. No center outside \(A\) has a nonzero reflected row. Each atom \(x\) can be an endpoint in exactly \(m-1\) pairs, where \(m\le3\) is the size of its parity class. Thus its endpoint indegree is at most two. Each parity class supplies at most three rows. A center may also be an endpoint of another row; none of these arguments excludes or separates those overlapping roles.

Let \(B\) be a nonempty subset of \(\mathcal J\) and fix a ball center \(c\) with \(\lVert x-c\rVert^2\le R^2\) for all \(x\in A\). Since \(u_j-j\) and \(v_j-j\) are nonzero opposite integer vectors,
$$
\frac{\lVert u_j-c\rVert^2+\lVert v_j-c\rVert^2}{2}
-\lVert j-c\rVert^2
=
\left\lVert\frac{u_j-v_j}{2}\right\rVert^2
\ge1.
\tag{6}
$$
Sum (6) over \(B\). For an atom \(x\in B\), its coefficient on the resulting right side is \(\deg_B(x)/2-1\le0\), where \(\deg_B(x)\) counts endpoint incidences from \(B\) to \(x\). For \(x\notin B\), the coefficient is \(\deg_B(x)/2\). Since squared norms are nonnegative, dropping the nonpositive contributions of atoms in \(B\) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
|B|
&\le
\frac12
\sum_{\substack{j\in B\\x\in\lbrace u_j,v_j\rbrace\setminus B}}
\lVert x-c\rVert^2\\
&\le\frac{R^2L(B)}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
$$
In particular, \(L(B)>0\). Finiteness of \(\mathcal J\) now proves that \(\mathfrak L(A)\) is defined, and (7) proves (1). A lattice-affine isomorphism preserves the endpoint pairs, centers, and the incidence counts in its definition. This proves the invariance assertion and also makes clear why the separate Euclidean radius bound is coordinate-dependent.

We next prove (2), using the same scalar energy as ee640ebdfbcb632d but a different global charge. Set \(t_x=Kp_x\) and let \(\theta_x=s_x\) for \(x\in\mathcal S\) and \(\theta_x=0\) otherwise. Define
$$
\Psi(t,\theta)
=t\bigl((1+2\theta)t-1\bigr)^2
+4\theta(1-\theta)t^2.
$$
It is nonnegative for \(t\ge0\) and \(0\le\theta\le1\), and
$$
\sum_{x\in A}\Psi(t_x,\theta_x)
=K\bigl(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\bigr).
\tag{8}
$$
Moreover,
$$
\Psi(t,\theta)
\ge t\min\lbrace(t-1)^2,(3t-1)^2\rbrace.
\tag{9}
$$
For completeness, its expansion is
$$
t(t-1)^2+4\theta t^3+4\theta^2t^2(t-1).
$$
When \(0\le t\le1\), it is concave in \(\theta\), so its minimum on \([0,1]\) is at an endpoint. Those endpoint values are \(t(t-1)^2\) and \(t(3t-1)^2\). When \(t\ge1\), the two \(\theta\)-dependent coefficients are nonnegative, and the first of those endpoint values is the smaller one. This proves (9).

Call a selected center near-resonant if
$$
s_j>\frac78
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac14<t_j<\frac49,
$$
and let \(B\) be the set of all these centers. We first charge \(\mathcal S\setminus B\) without any graph argument. Rows with \(s_j\le7/8\) have \(\beta_j\le2\) times their contribution to \(\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\), where \(\beta_j=Ks_jp_j^2\), exactly as in ee640ebdfbcb632d. If \(s_j>7/8\) and \(t_j\le1/4\), its own deviation term is at least \(t_j/16\), so
$$
s_jt_j^2\le4\Psi(t_j,\theta_j).
$$
If \(s_j>7/8\) and \(t_j\ge4/9\), then
$$
(1+2s_j)t_j-1\ge\frac{t_j}{2},
$$
and its deviation term is at least \(t_j^3/4\ge t_j^2/9\). Hence
$$
s_jt_j^2\le9\Psi(t_j,\theta_j).
$$
Summing these disjoint cases and using (8) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{\mathcal S\setminus B}
&\le2\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}
+9\bigl(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\bigr)\\
&\le11\bigl(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
$$

Here is the required local propagation estimate. For a parity class \(\eta\), put
$$
d_\eta
=\left(\sum_{\substack{x\in A\\x\equiv\eta\pmod2}}t_x-1\right)^2,
$$
so \(\sum_\eta d_\eta=K\mathcal D\). The subscripted scalar \(d_\eta\) is a parity-mass error, not the continuous dimension \(d\) of the locked problem. Suppose \(j\in B\), let \(\eta\) be its source endpoint parity, and fix either endpoint \(x\) of its pair. If
$$
d_\eta<2^{-12}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Psi(t_x,\theta_x)<2^{-20},
\tag{11}
$$
then \(x\in B\). To prove this, write
$$
\xi=t_j,\qquad
\upsilon=t_{u_j},\qquad
\omega=t_{v_j}.
$$
Their exact product satisfies
$$
\upsilon\omega=s_j^2\xi^2>\frac{49}{1024}.
$$
The source parity mass in \(t\)-coordinates is less than \(65/64\) by (11), so \(\upsilon+\omega<65/64\), even if the class has a third atom. Both endpoints are therefore less than \(65/64\) and greater than
$$
\frac{49/1024}{65/64}=\frac{49}{1040}>\frac1{32}.
$$
By (9), the second inequality of (11) implies
$$
\min\lbrace(t_x-1)^2,(3t_x-1)^2\rbrace
<2^{-15}<2^{-14}.
$$
Thus \(t_x\) is in either \((127/128,129/128)\) or \((127/384,129/384)\). The first interval is impossible: the other endpoint is greater than \(1/32\), so the sum of the two endpoints would exceed
$$
\frac{127}{128}+\frac1{32}
=\frac{131}{128}>\frac{65}{64}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{127}{384}<t_x<\frac{129}{384}.
$$
If \(\theta_x\le7/8\), then
$$
(1+2\theta_x)t_x
<\frac{11}{4}\frac{129}{384}
=\frac{473}{512}.
$$
Its deviation energy would consequently exceed \((1/4)(1/16)^2=2^{-10}\), contradicting (11). Hence \(\theta_x>7/8\). This implies \(x\in\mathcal S\) and \(s_x>7/8\), and the last interval lies within \((1/4,4/9)\), proving \(x\in B\). This argument only needed the small energy of the endpoint under consideration; the other endpoint's energy was unrestricted.

Apply the contrapositive to each incidence \(j\to x\) leaving \(B\). Its contribution of one is at most
$$
2^{12}d_\eta+2^{20}\Psi(t_x,\theta_x).
$$
Each row has two outgoing incidences, each source parity class has at most three rows, and each target atom has endpoint indegree at most two. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
L(B)
&\le6\cdot2^{12}\sum_\eta d_\eta
+2\cdot2^{20}\sum_x\Psi(t_x,\theta_x)\\
&=3\cdot2^{13}K\mathcal D
+2^{21}K\bigl(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
$$
This counts all center/endpoint overlaps through their actual indegrees. It does not assume singleton endpoint rows.

If \(B=\varnothing\), its intensity is zero. Otherwise \(s_jt_j^2<16/81<1/4\) on \(B\), and the definition of \(\mathfrak L(A)\), followed by (12), gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_B
&\le\frac{|B|}{4K}
\le\frac{\mathfrak L(A)L(B)}{8K}\\
&\le\mathfrak L(A)
\left[
3\cdot2^{10}\mathcal D
+2^{18}\bigl(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\bigr)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
$$
Combining (10) and (13), and using \(3\cdot2^{10}\le2\cdot2^{18}\), proves
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{\mathcal S}
&\le
\bigl(11+2^{18}\mathfrak L(A)\bigr)
\bigl(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\bigr)
+3\cdot2^{10}\mathfrak L(A)\mathcal D\\
&\le
\bigl(11+2^{18}\mathfrak L(A)\bigr)\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Together with (1), this proves both inequalities in (2), including empty \(\mathcal J\) and empty selections.

We prove the uniform reduction rather than assuming that the matching energy identity stops holding at parity size three. For arbitrary weights in the present setting, expanding every parity square includes exactly one cross term for every unordered pair, and conditions (ii)-(iii) identify those pairs with \(\mathcal J\). Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_\eta r_\eta^2
&=\sum_xp_x^2+2\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}s_j^2p_j^2,\\
\widehat\chi_{\mathcal S}
&=\sum_xp_x^2+2\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}s_jp_j^2,
\end{aligned}
$$
where \(\widehat\chi_{\mathcal S}=\sum_xp_x\widehat H_{\mathcal S}(x)\) and \(\widehat b_{\mathcal S}=\sum_xp_x\widehat H_{\mathcal S}(x)^2\), with exactly the selected-row meanings of ee640ebdfbcb632d. Since
$$
\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}
=K^2\widehat b_{\mathcal S}-2K\widehat\chi_{\mathcal S}+1,
$$
substitution into the definitions proves
$$
K^2\widehat b_{\mathcal S}
=1+\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}
-4K\sum_{j\in\mathcal J\setminus\mathcal S}s_j^2p_j^2.
\tag{14}
$$
Thus the normalization identity of ee640ebdfbcb632d remains exact here, although its matching incidence charge does not apply.

Under the uniform law, every \(s_j=1\). A supported center \(j\in\mathcal J\) has \(H_p(j)=3/N\); each of the \(t\) other supported centers has \(H_p(j)=1/N\). Hence there are \(N-t\) nontrivial rows, and direct summation gives \(\chi\) and \(b\) in (3). The full-row version of (14) gives
$$
\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}=K^2b(p)-1,
\qquad
\beta_{\mathcal J}=\frac{K(N-t)}{N^2}.
$$
Factoring \(9K^2N-N^3\) as \((3K-N)N(3K+N)\) proves the last expression in (3).

There are \(m_2+3m_3\) unordered distinct same-parity pairs, so midpoint injectivity gives \(N-t=m_2+3m_3\). Subtract this from \(N=m_1+2m_2+3m_3\) to obtain \(t=m_1+m_2\). Since \(K=m_0+m_1+m_2+m_3\), subtraction also gives
$$
\Delta=3m_0+2m_1+m_2=t+3m_0+m_1,
$$
proving (4). At least one vertex of \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) exists, and a vertex cannot be a midpoint of two distinct points of \(A\). Thus \(t\ge1\), and (4) gives \(\Delta>0\). In particular, exact global zero-defect resonance cannot occur for a finite support.

For \(2K\le N<3K\), write \(\vartheta=N/K\in[2,3)\), \(\varepsilon_A=3-\vartheta\), and \(u=t/K\). By (4), \(0\le u\le\varepsilon_A\). Formula (3) becomes
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{\mathcal J}
&=\frac{\vartheta-u}{\vartheta^2},\\
\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}
&=\frac{\varepsilon_A\vartheta(\vartheta+3)-8u}{\vartheta^3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
$$
It follows that
$$
\beta_{\mathcal J}\le\frac1\vartheta\le\frac12,
\qquad
\beta_{\mathcal J}\ge\frac{2\vartheta-3}{\vartheta^2}\ge\frac14.
$$
For the lower energy bound, use \(u\le\varepsilon_A\) and
$$
4(\vartheta^2+3\vartheta-8)-\vartheta^3
=(\vartheta-2)(16+2\vartheta-\vartheta^2)\ge0.
$$
For the upper energy bound, use \(u\ge0\) and
$$
5\vartheta^2-4\vartheta-12
=(\vartheta-2)(5\vartheta+6)\ge0.
$$
These give \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}\ge\varepsilon_A/4\) and \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}\le5\varepsilon_A/4\), respectively. Combining the four bounds proves (5).

For \(N\le2K\), the conclusion is immediate if \(\mathcal J=\varnothing\). Otherwise put \(\vartheta=N/K\in(0,2]\) and \(\gamma_{\mathcal J}=|\mathcal J|/K>0\). This normalized row count is distinct from the canonical ratio \(a(p)\). Directly from (3),
$$
\frac{\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}}{\beta_{\mathcal J}}
=\frac8\vartheta+\frac{1-\vartheta^2}{\gamma_{\mathcal J}}.
$$
For \(\vartheta\le1\), this is at least \(8/\vartheta\ge8\). For \(1<\vartheta\le2\), the parity census gives \(|\mathcal J|\ge N-K\), so \(\gamma_{\mathcal J}\ge\vartheta-1\). Consequently,
$$
\frac{\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}}{\beta_{\mathcal J}}
\ge\frac8\vartheta-(\vartheta+1)\ge1.
$$
This proves \(\beta_{\mathcal J}\le\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}\) for \(N\le2K\). If \(\beta_{\mathcal J}\le C\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}\) holds throughout a collection, (5) forces \(\Delta/K\ge1/(5C)\) on its supports with \(N\ge2K\); its remaining supports have \(\Delta/K\ge1\). Conversely, a gap \(\Delta/K\ge\varepsilon_0>0\), together with (5) and the \(N\le2K\) estimate, gives the uniform charge with
$$
C=\max\lbrace1,2/\varepsilon_0\rbrace.
$$
This proves the claimed equivalence.

The accepted defect normalization and its limitation can now be checked exactly. For a lattice-convex \(A\), accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7 gives the oriented zero-inclusive reflection convention used here and \(v\le t\), while the sharper equality audit in 44636aeaf6af4b6c records the nonnegative parity and nonvertex deficits. In the notation of 4e40b39340899863,
$$
e=t-v\ge0,
\qquad
\delta=3K-N-v=(3m_0+m_1)+e.
$$
Hence \(\Delta=v+\delta\), as stated. These identities only require the actual counts, not a lower bound proportional to \(K\). The bound \(v\ge n+1\) for full dimension consequently yields \(\Delta\ge n+1\). The resulting lower bound \((n+1)/K\) tends to zero and supplies no absolute census gap.

There are actual supports with all the hypotheses, so this obstruction is not merely a local algebraic resonance calculation. The accepted twenty-point tetrahedron 768d9712b73c4ab7 has \(K=8\), \(N=20\), and \(t=4\). Formula (3) gives
$$
\beta_{\mathcal J}=\frac8{25},
\qquad
\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}=\frac{23}{125},
\qquad
\frac{\beta_{\mathcal J}}{\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}}=\frac{40}{23}.
$$
Any universal charge constant on the present class must therefore be at least \(40/23\). The distinct midpoint and parity certificates in that fact verify (i)-(iii). The accepted thirty-six-point support 3dd581471de351a8 has \(K=16\), \(N=36\), \(t=8\), and parity sizes at most three with distinct pair midpoints. Its values are
$$
\beta_{\mathcal J}=\frac{28}{81},
\qquad
\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}=\frac{311}{729}.
$$
All four singleton parity classes of that support consist of reflection-three points. Thus replacing \(t\) by the singleton parity count in (3) or in the defect charge would be incorrect on an actual lattice-convex support.

Finally, the sufficient condition in 4e40b39340899863, if realized at every step, gives lattice-convex supports with parity sizes at most three, reflection maximum three,
$$
N=3K-O(n^2),
\qquad
t=O(n^2).
$$
Reflection maximum three and midpoint closure imply distinct pair midpoints, so these conditional supports would satisfy every present support hypothesis. Formula (5) would then give
$$
\frac{\beta_{\mathcal J}}{\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}}
\ge\frac{K}{5\Delta}\longrightarrow\infty.
$$
This is a conditional obstruction to a dimension-free intensity charge, not an existence claim and not a depth counterexample.

The finite geometric coefficient degenerates on the same conditional sequence for a separate exact reason. Every incidence leaving \(\mathcal J\) lands at one of the \(t\) singleton-row atoms, whose endpoint indegree is at most two. Thus \(L(\mathcal J)\le2t\) and, when \(\mathcal J\ne\varnothing\),
$$
\mathfrak L(A)
\ge\frac{2|\mathcal J|}{L(\mathcal J)}
\ge\frac{N-t}{t}.
\tag{16}
$$
In particular, (1) and (16) force \(R^2\ge(N-t)/t\) for every enclosing ball in the chosen coordinates. The finite geometric argument therefore cannot silently produce a dimension-free constant on that sequence. Conversely, a universal lower bound on \(L(B)/|B|\) for every nonempty \(B\subseteq\mathcal J\) is precisely the quantitative step that would bound \(\mathfrak L(A)\) and turn (2) into the full weighted charge. No such bound is proved here. Equations (5), (16), and the conditional status of the accepted lift isolate why finite geometric resonance exclusion alone does not settle the general bridge.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\), \(K=2^n\), and let \(A\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be finite and nonempty, satisfying all three conditions:

(i) Every coordinatewise parity class has at most three members of \(A\).

(ii) The midpoint of every distinct same-parity pair of members of \(A\) belongs to \(A\).

(iii) Different unordered distinct same-parity pairs have different midpoints.

Let \(\mathcal J\) be the set of these midpoints. For \(j\in\mathcal J\), write \(\lbrace u_j,v_j\rbrace\) for its unique endpoint pair. Form the directed midpoint graph with the two endpoint incidences \(j\to u_j\) and \(j\to v_j\) for every \(j\in\mathcal J\). For nonempty \(B\subseteq\mathcal J\), let \(L(B)\) be the number of these incidences having source in \(B\) and target outside \(B\). If \(\mathcal J\ne\varnothing\), define
$$
\mathfrak L(A)
=\max_{\varnothing\ne B\subseteq\mathcal J}\frac{2|B|}{L(B)}.
$$
If \(\mathcal J=\varnothing\), set \(\mathfrak L(A)=0\). All denominators in the displayed maximum are positive. The graph coefficient \(\mathfrak L(A)\) is a new scalar; it is not the mixed lattice \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\) of the locked problem. In the original Euclidean coordinates, if \(A\) is contained in a ball of radius \(R\) with any real center, then
$$
\mathfrak L(A)\le R^2. \tag{1}
$$
This radius is a coordinate-dependent quantity. In particular, \(R\) need not be dimension-free, and its value need not be preserved by a unimodular change of coordinates. The coefficient \(\mathfrak L(A)\) depends only on the midpoint incidences and is preserved by lattice-affine isomorphisms.

Use exactly the normalization of accepted fact ee640ebdfbcb632d: choose \(w_x>0\), put \(Z=\sum_{x\in A}w_x\) and \(p_x=w_x/Z\), extend \(p\) by zero outside \(A\), and suppose
$$
p_j\ge\sqrt{p_{u_j}p_{v_j}}
\qquad(j\in\mathcal J).
$$
The canonical quantities remain
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_p(x)&=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\sqrt{p_{x+v}p_{x-v}},\\
b(p)&=\sum_xp_xH_p(x)^2,
&\chi(p)&=\sum_xp_xH_p(x).
\end{aligned}
$$
In particular, the atom sum \(A_0=K^2\sum_xp_x^3\) is not the canonical ratio \(a(p)=\chi(p)/b(p)\). The actual ambient closed-halfspace depths \(\tau_p\) and their moments \(M_2\) and \(M_3\) retain their meanings in ee640ebdfbcb632d; no depth or moment conclusion is asserted here.

For every \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal J\), define
$$
\begin{aligned}
s_j&=\frac{\sqrt{p_{u_j}p_{v_j}}}{p_j}\in(0,1],\\
\widehat H_{\mathcal S}(x)
&=
\begin{cases}
(1+2s_x)p_x,&x\in\mathcal S,\\
p_x,&x\notin\mathcal S,
\end{cases}\\
r_\eta&=\sum_{\substack{x\in A\\x\equiv\eta\pmod2}}p_x,\\
\mathcal D&=K\sum_\eta r_\eta^2-1,\\
\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}
&=\sum_xp_x\bigl(K\widehat H_{\mathcal S}(x)-1\bigr)^2,\\
\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}
&=4K\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}s_j(1-s_j)p_j^2,\\
\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}
&=\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+2\mathcal D+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S},\\
\beta_{\mathcal S}
&=K\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}s_jp_j^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
The sums over \(\eta\) include all \(K\) ambient parity classes. These are precisely the selected-row deviation energy, parity energy, ratio energy, and intensity of ee640ebdfbcb632d, now on the stated three-point parity supports. Then
$$
\beta_{\mathcal S}
\le\bigl(11+2^{18}\mathfrak L(A)\bigr)\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}
\le\bigl(11+2^{18}R^2\bigr)\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}.
\tag{2}
$$

For the uniform law \(p_x=1/N\) on \(A\), where \(N=|A|\), and the full selection \(\mathcal S=\mathcal J\), let \(t=|A\setminus\mathcal J|\) and \(\Delta=3K-N\). Then \(\Delta>0\) and
$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi(p)&=\frac{3N-2t}{N^2},
&b(p)&=\frac{9N-8t}{N^3},\\
\beta_{\mathcal J}&=\frac{K(N-t)}{N^2},\\
\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}
&=\frac{K^2(9N-8t)}{N^3}-1\\
&=\frac{\Delta N(3K+N)-8K^2t}{N^3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$
If \(m_i\) counts the ambient parity classes of size \(i\), for \(0\le i\le3\), then
$$
t=m_1+m_2,
\qquad
\Delta=t+3m_0+m_1.
\tag{4}
$$
If \(2K\le N<3K\), put \(\varepsilon_A=\Delta/K\). This normalized census deficit is distinct from the continuous dimension \(d\) of the locked problem. The exact uniform formulas imply
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\varepsilon_A}{4}
&\le\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}
\le\frac{5\varepsilon_A}{4},
&
\frac14&\le\beta_{\mathcal J}\le\frac12,\\
\frac{K}{5\Delta}
&\le\frac{\beta_{\mathcal J}}{\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}}
\le\frac{2K}{\Delta}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
$$
For \(N\le2K\), one instead has \(\beta_{\mathcal J}\le\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}\). Consequently, on any collection of supports satisfying (i)-(iii), a dimension-free uniform full-row charge \(\beta_{\mathcal J}\le C\mathcal E_{\mathcal J}\) exists if and only if there is an absolute \(\varepsilon_0>0\) with \(N\le(3-\varepsilon_0)K\) throughout that collection. This equivalence concerns the uniform full-row charge; it does not assert that a uniform census gap suffices for arbitrary weights or selections.

For lattice-convex supports, the exact map to the defect notation of accepted fact 4e40b39340899863 is
$$
v=|\operatorname{vert}(\operatorname{conv}(A))|,
\qquad
e=t-v,
\qquad
\delta=3K-N-v,
\qquad
\Delta=v+\delta,
$$
with \(\delta=(3m_0+m_1)+e\). Thus (5) is an exact reduction to the total canonical deficit, rather than an identification of singleton parity classes with reflection-one points. Accepted facts 768d9712b73c4ab7 and 3dd581471de351a8 give actual finite calibrations, and accepted facts 44636aeaf6af4b6c and 4e40b39340899863 supply the vertex-budget and conditional near-saturation comparisons detailed below.
